{{Short description| Many-body of charged particles}}

In [[statistical physics]], a '''Coulomb gas''' is a [[many-body system]] of [[charged particles]] interacting under the [[electrostatic force]]. It is named after [[Charles-Augustin de Coulomb]], as the force by which the particles interact is also known as the Coulomb force.

The system can be defined in any number of dimensions. While the three-dimensional Coulomb gas is the most experimentally realistic, the best understood is the two-dimensional Coulomb gas. The two-dimensional Coulomb gas is known to be equivalent to the continuum [[XY model]] of magnets and the [[sine-Gordon model]] (upon taking certain limits) in a physical sense, in that physical observables ([[correlation functions]]) calculated in one model can be used to calculate physical observables in another model. This aided the understanding of the [[BKT transition]], and the discoverers earned a [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] for their work on this [[phase transition]].<ref name="KT">{{cite journal 
|last1=Kosterlitz |first1=J M 
|last2=Thouless |first2=D J 
|title=Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems 
|journal=Journal of Physics C: Solid State Physics |date=12 April 1973 
|volume=6 |issue=7 |pages=1181–1203 
|doi=10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010 
|bibcode=1973JPhC....6.1181K 
|url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010 
|access-date=28 July 2023|url-access=subscription 
}}</ref>

== Formulation ==
Define the function ('''Coulomb kernel''', or '''Riesz kernel''')<math display="block">\begin{align}
g_s(x) = 
\begin{cases}-\log|x| & \text{ if } s = 0, \\
 \frac{1}{s|x|^{s}} & \text{ if } s \neq 0
\end{cases}
\end{align}</math>The setup starts with considering <math>N</math> charged particles in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> with positions <math>\mathbf{r}_i</math> and charges <math>q_i</math>. From [[electrostatics]], the pairwise potential energy between particles labelled by indices <math>i,j</math> is (up to scale factor)
<math display="block">V_{ij} = q_iq_jg_{d-2}(|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j|),</math>where <math>g_{d-2}(x)</math> is the '''Coulomb kernel''' or [[Green's function]] of the [[Laplace equation]] in <math>d</math> dimensions.<ref>{{cite arXiv
	| last = Chafaï
	| first = Djalil
	| author-link = 
	| date = 24 August 2021
	| title = Aspects of Coulomb gases
	| eprint = 2108.10653
	| class = math.PR
}}</ref> The [[thermodynamic free energy|free energy]] due to these interactions is then (proportional to) <math>F = \sum_{i \neq j} V_{ij}</math>, and the [[partition function (statistical mechanics)|partition function]] is given by integrating over different configurations, that is, the positions of the charged particles.

More generally, any choice of <math>s \in [d-2, d)</math> makes sense. This general case is called '''Riesz gas''', of which the Coulomb gas is a special case. The naming comes from the fact that the Riesz kernel is the Green's function of the [[fractional Laplacian]], which can be defined using the [[Riesz potential]]. Specifically,<ref name=":0">{{cite arXiv | last1=Serfaty | first1=Sylvia | title=Lectures on Coulomb and Riesz gases | date=2024 | class=math-ph | eprint=2407.21194 }}</ref><math display="block">(-\Delta)^{\frac{d-s}2} g_s = c_{d, s} \delta_0</math>where <math display="block">c_{d, s} = \begin{cases}\frac{2^{d-s} \pi^{d / 2} \Gamma\left(\frac{d-s}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)} & \text { for } s>\max (0, d-2) \\ \frac{2 \pi^{d / 2}}{\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)}=\left|\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\right| & \text { if } s=d-2>0 \\ 2 \pi & \text { if } s=0, d=1 \text { or } d=2\end{cases}
</math>

== Names ==
When there is only one type of charge (conventionally assumed positive), it is called a '''one-component [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]]'''. Sometimes there is an additional background charge distribution that cancels out the charge on average. For example, in the case of the [[Ginibre ensemble]], the background charge would be the uniform distribution on the unit disk. With such a neutralizing background, it is called a '''[[jellium]]'''.<ref name=":0" />

When <math>d = 2, s = 0</math>, i is called a log gas, two-dimensional one-component plasma (2DOCP), two-dimensional jellium, or Dyson gas.<ref name=":0" />

== Coulomb gas in conformal field theory ==
The two-dimensional Coulomb gas can be used as a framework for describing fields in [[minimal model (physics)|minimal model]]s. This comes from the similarity of the two-point [[correlation function]] of the free boson <math>\varphi</math>,
<math display = block>\langle \varphi(z, \bar z) \varphi(w, \bar w) \rangle = - \log|z - w|^2</math>
to the electric potential energy between two unit charges in two dimensions.<ref name="BYB">{{cite book 
|last1=Di Francesco |first1=Philippe 
|last2=Mathieu |first2=Pierre 
|last3=Sénéchal |first3=David 
|title=Conformal Field Theory |series=Graduate Texts in Contemporary Physics 
|date=1997 
|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-2256-9 
|isbn=978-1-4612-7475-9 
|url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4612-2256-9 
|access-date=22 August 2023 |language=en}}</ref>
